summary: Kole Jain names three flaws that show a designer has never built a real dashboard, and how to fix each. First, the data should drive the form: columns with a fixed set of values become chips, numbers are right-aligned, long text is truncated, inactive rows are shaded, time-based data becomes a timeline, and color comes from what the data means rather than decoration. Second, hierarchy is also about what you show and hide (progressive disclosure): rarely used features go into popovers, secondary actions appear on hover, and onboarding sequences features, starting with a single tooltip, instead of explaining everything at once. Third, much of a finished product is UI you cannot see at first, such as copy chips over cells, comment indicators, hidden states and tooltips, which beginner dashboards almost always miss. For a design system, this gives rules for table and data display, a 'spectrum of explicitness' for deciding how visible an action should be, and a reminder to design hidden states and tooltips as part of every component.
key_ideas: Dashboards exist to display data, so the UI should be shaped around the data it shows.
Columns that only have a set number of values, like department or employment status, read better as chips.
Right-aligning numbers lines digits up by place value.
Truncating long text frees room for the other columns, and shading inactive or deactivated rows sets them apart.
Data that is split by time may not belong in a table at all; a timeline is easier to follow than a time-sorted table.
Landing pages can get away with a lot, but dashboard color should come from the data, such as red for an urgent action.
Avatars let the eye link who did what faster than reading a name, and a chart can summarise data that has a time dimension.
Progressive disclosure is a kind of hierarchy based on what you show and what you hide.
The spectrum of explicitness runs from a global, always-visible button (high) to an icon that appears on hover (low).
Onboarding is progressive disclosure: sequence features so the user is never overwhelmed, rather than hiding them.
A dense design gets its extra functionality from UI you cannot immediately see, and there is a lot of it.
New features often do not need a dedicated page; they need to be better thought through in how they are implemented.
Putting the pieces together (spacing, sizing) is not that hard; orchestrating them, including components with hidden parts and states, takes thought.
Tooltips are missing on nearly all beginner dashboards; assume users will not understand every icon or ambiguous label.

topics.name: Dashboards and data display
topics.summary: Let the data drive the form: chips for fixed-value columns, right-aligned numbers, truncated long text, shaded inactive rows, timelines for time-based data, and summary charts for data with a time dimension.

topics.name: Visual hierarchy
topics.summary: Besides strong versus poor hierarchy in a card, there is hierarchy by what you show and hide (progressive disclosure), placed along a spectrum of explicitness.

topics.name: Onboarding
topics.summary: Start with a single tooltip on the most important action, then a second one or a simple checklist in a corner; avoid a login modal that explains the whole product in six bullet points.

topics.name: Modals and popovers
topics.summary: Put infrequent features like sharing into a popover rather than a permanent panel or a new page; put the popover's primary action (a search box) at the top and reveal secondary actions on hover.

topics.name: Color
topics.summary: In dashboards, color should come from the data itself, for example a red icon in a chip to draw the eye to an urgent action, not be sprinkled in to look nice.

topics.name: Icons and imagery
topics.summary: Avatars in activity logs speed up recognising who did what; icons need tooltips because users will not understand all of them.

topics.name: Gestures and drag
topics.summary: Apple Reminders reveals secondary actions on swipe left and right, keeping the main action (checking off a reminder) primary.

topics.name: AI-assisted design
topics.summary: The presenter says AI struggles with the idea that UI is as much about what you cannot see as what you can.

rules.rule: Display table columns that have a fixed set of values, such as department or employment status, as chips.
rules.why: There is only a set number of departments or employment statuses, and chips let the data drive the form.
rules.evidence: turned the department and employment into chips

rules.why: Digits then align by place value.
rules.evidence: right align the numbers so the digits align by place value

rules.rule: Truncate long text in table cells.
rules.why: It gives more breathing room to the other columns.
rules.evidence: truncating long text to give more breathing room

rules.rule: Shade out table rows that are inactive or deactivated.
rules.why: It lets the row's status shape how the table looks, part of letting the data drive the form.
rules.evidence: shade out rows of the table that are inactive or deactivated

rules.rule: Show time-delineated data as a timeline, placed in a sidebar pop-out or as a wider second column beside the table, instead of a time-sorted table.
rules.why: A timeline is a lot easier to follow and lets the data determine the shape of the UI.
rules.evidence: if we were to arrange this as a timeline

rules.rule: Do not add color to a dashboard for decoration; derive it from the data, such as a red icon in a chip for an urgent action.
rules.why: Dashboard color should come from the data itself; the red draws the eye because the action is urgent.
rules.evidence: dashboard colors shouldn't just be sprinkled in to look nice

rules.rule: Show an avatar next to the actor in activity logs.
rules.why: The eye associates who did what much faster than by reading a name in the column.
rules.evidence: The avatar is there because your eye can associate who did what

rules.rule: Add a summary chart when the data has a time dimension.
rules.why: The chart shows the change over time instantly instead of making users hunt through a timestamp column.
rules.evidence: adding a chart to roll up the data into a summary

rules.rule: Put infrequently used features, such as sharing, in a popover rather than permanently in the layout or on a separate page.
rules.why: They are not accessed often or important enough to be always visible, and a popover avoids taking the user to an entirely different page.
rules.evidence: we tuck it into a popover so we don't have to rip the user to an entirely different page

rules.rule: Place a popover's primary action, such as the search box in a share popover, at the top where it is immediately visible.
rules.why: It is the primary action of the popover.
rules.evidence: the primary action is of course the search box

rules.rule: When space is tight, reveal secondary actions such as removing a user as an icon on hover, with a tooltip.
rules.why: The action is not a main one, so it is progressively revealed as soon as the user starts to look for it.
rules.evidence: we show the remove button on hover along with a tooltip

rules.rule: Onboard new users with a single tooltip pointing at the most important action, then a second tooltip or a simple checklist in the corner once they have done it.
rules.why: Sequencing features means the user is never overwhelmed, without hiding functionality.
rules.evidence: A good onboarding might start with a single tooltip

rules.rule: Do not explain the entire product in a modal of bullet points the moment a user first logs in, and do not drop first-time users onto a fully loaded dashboard.
rules.why: Users forget the modal instantly once they dismiss it, and a fully loaded dashboard leaves them wondering where to start.
rules.evidence: explaining the entire product in a modal with six bullet points

rules.rule: Add tooltips to icons and to ambiguous labels.
rules.why: Assume users will not understand all of the icons, or may want more detail; tooltips are missing on nearly all beginner dashboards.
rules.evidence: what's missing pretty much unequivocally on all beginner dashboards are tooltips

rules.rule: Design the hidden UI of dense components, such as a copy chip over table cells on hover and a small triangle indicator for comments, along with the hidden components and states of drawers and modals.
rules.why: In a dense design, additional functionality has to come from parts of the UI you cannot immediately see, and the table needs all of it to function.
rules.evidence: a copy chip over the cells or perhaps comment functionality with a small triangle indicator

rules.rule: Before giving a new feature its own page, check whether it can live in existing UI through hidden components and states, such as those of a drawer or modal.
rules.why: New features or elements often don't require a dedicated page, just to be better thought through in how they are implemented.
rules.evidence: new features or elements often don't require a dedicated page

rules.rule: Design the rarely seen moments too, such as new-feature announcements and onboarding pop-ups that explain part of the product.
rules.why: There is a lot of hidden UI that is important for a finished product.
rules.evidence: Think about moments in software that you almost never see

rules.rule: Place each action on the spectrum of explicitness by how important and frequently used it is: a global, always-visible button (such as share) sits high, and a minor action (such as copying a cell) can be an icon revealed on hover.
rules.why: The spectrum runs from a global, always-visible share button (quite high) to an icon to copy a cell on hover (much lower); actions that are not frequently accessed or not main actions are revealed progressively.
rules.evidence: what I've just described is called the spectrum of explicitness

rules.rule: Consider revealing useful but secondary list-item actions on swipe left and right, as Apple Reminders does, keeping them apart from the primary action of checking the item off.
rules.why: The source cites it as progressive disclosure done really well: swiping reveals useful but secondary actions compared to checking off the reminder.
rules.evidence: On swipe left and right, it reveals useful but secondary actions

decisions.question: How should a table column with only a few possible values, like department or status, be shown?

options.name: Plain text
options.effect: The table looks logically laid out, but nothing is driving the form.
options.when: Not recommended by the source for fixed-value columns.

options.name: Chips
options.effect: The table starts to shape up around its data.
options.when: When there is only a set number of possible values.

decisions.recommendation: Chips, because there is only a set number of departments or employment statuses.
decisions.evidence: turned the department and employment into chips

decisions.question: How should data that is ordered by time be displayed?

options.name: Time-sorted table
options.effect: Works and can be used, but is harder to follow and does not let the data shape the UI.
options.when: The source says it works but is not the best format.

options.name: Timeline in a sidebar pop-out
options.effect: Easier to follow, tucked away beside the main view.
options.when: When the time-based view is secondary to the table [inferred].

options.name: Timeline as a wider second column beside the table
options.effect: Easier to follow and shown alongside the table.
options.when: When there is room and the timeline deserves to be visible [inferred].

decisions.recommendation: A timeline, in either placement, so the data drives the UI.
decisions.evidence: the time delineated nature means that this isn't the best format

decisions.question: How should color be used on a dashboard?

options.name: Decorative color sprinkled in to look nice
options.effect: Sprinkled in to look nice rather than coming from the data.
options.when: Landing pages can get away with this; dashboards should not.

options.name: Color that comes from the data
options.effect: Color draws the eye to what matters, such as a red icon in a chip for an urgent action.

decisions.question: How visible should a secondary action be (where does it sit on the spectrum of explicitness)?

options.name: Icon revealed on hover, with a tooltip
options.effect: Low on the spectrum: saves space, and the action is revealed as soon as the user starts to look for it.
options.when: Space is tight and the action is not a main one, such as removing a user from sharing or copying a cell.

options.name: Icon always visible
options.effect: More explicit; the action is always on screen.
options.when: When the action should be more explicit and space allows [inferred].

options.name: Always visible with a full text label
options.effect: Still more explicit; the action is spelled out.
options.when: When the action should be as explicit as possible [inferred].

options.name: Global, always-visible button
options.effect: Quite high on the spectrum, like a global, always-visible share button.

decisions.recommendation: For a secondary action with little space, reveal it on hover with a tooltip.
decisions.evidence: what I've just described is called the spectrum of explicitness

decisions.question: Where should an infrequently used feature, like sharing, live?

options.name: Permanently in the side of the table
options.effect: Permanently ingrained in the layout for something not frequently accessed or important enough.
options.when: The source advises against it for infrequent features.

options.name: A separate page
options.effect: Rips the user away to an entirely different page.
options.when: The source advises against it here.

options.name: A popover
options.effect: Available in context without leaving the page; its primary action sits at the top.
options.when: The feature is not frequently accessed or important enough to be always visible.

decisions.recommendation: A popover, because sharing is not frequently accessed and a popover avoids a page change.
decisions.evidence: this share functionality isn't permanently ingrained in the side of the table

decisions.question: How should first-time users be introduced to the product?

options.name: A fully loaded dashboard with no guidance
options.effect: Users stare at it wondering where to start.

options.name: A modal explaining the whole product at login
options.effect: Six bullet points that are forgotten the moment the modal is dismissed.

options.name: Sequenced tooltips and a checklist
options.effect: A single tooltip on the most important action, then a second one or a simple checklist in the corner; the user is never overwhelmed.

decisions.recommendation: Sequence features with tooltips and a simple checklist so the user is never overwhelmed.
decisions.evidence: A good onboarding might start with a single tooltip pointing at the most important action

process.detail: Focus on the data the dashboard has to display and build the UI around it, so the data drives the form.

process.step: Shape each column to its data
process.detail: Turn fixed-value columns into chips, right-align numbers, truncate long text and shade inactive or deactivated rows.
If the data is split by time, consider a timeline in a sidebar pop-out or a second column instead of a time-sorted table.
Use color that comes from the data (red for urgent), avatars for who did what, and a summary chart when the data has a time dimension.

process.step: Place actions on the spectrum of explicitness
process.detail: Keep main actions visible, move infrequent features into popovers with the primary action at the top, and reveal secondary actions on hover with a tooltip.
Add hover copy chips, comment indicators, tooltips for icons and ambiguous labels, and the hidden states of drawers and modals; plan announcements and onboarding pop-ups.
Start with one tooltip on the most important action, then a second tooltip or a simple checklist in the corner.
Put the original and revised versions side by side to see which is letting the data drive the form.
Look at a lot of real software to get a feel for progressive disclosure, the spectrum of explicitness and onboarding flows (this advice leads into the sponsor read).

examples.what: Table with department and employment status columns, before and after
examples.visual_note: The before is a logically laid out table where nothing drives the form; the after turns department and employment status into chips, right-aligns numbers, truncates long text and shades inactive rows.

examples.what: Time-sorted table turned into a timeline
examples.visual_note: Time-delineated records shown as a timeline, either tucked into a sidebar pop-out or as a wider second column beside the table.

examples.what: Activity log with meaningful color and avatars
examples.visual_note: A red icon in a chip flags an urgent action, avatars show who did what, and a chart rolls the log up into a summary over time.

examples.what: Card with poor versus strong hierarchy
examples.visual_note: Mentioned briefly as the usual way hierarchy is shown, before introducing hierarchy by showing and hiding.
Sharing opens in a popover from the table; a search box sits at the top as the primary action, and a remove button appears on hover with a tooltip.
Swiping left and right reveals useful but secondary actions, while checking off a reminder stays the primary action.

examples.what: Ends of the spectrum of explicitness
examples.visual_note: A global, always-visible share button is high on the spectrum; an icon to copy a cell on hover is low.

examples.what: Visible versus hidden UI of a dense table
examples.visual_note: The video overlays everything visible and then all the hidden UI (copy chip over cells, comment triangle indicator, states); the hidden part is not a small amount.

examples.what: Onboarding with a single tooltip and a checklist
examples.visual_note: A first tooltip points at the most important action, followed by a second tooltip or a simple checklist in a corner, contrasted with a login modal of six bullet points.

numbers.context: Dashboard flaws covered: data driving the form, the right things hidden until needed, and the invisible UI that makes it function.
numbers.evidence: those are the three subtle flaws

numbers.context: The anti-pattern onboarding modal that explains the entire product at login.
numbers.evidence: a modal with six bullet points the second you log in

caveats: Sponsor segment for Mobbin (auto-captions say 'Mavin'): hundreds of thousands of curated screens, a new MCP, a banking mood board made in about 2 minutes, and 20% off; excluded from rules. The advice to study real software leads directly into this read.

No exact values are given: no spacing, sizes, colors, row heights, hover delays or tooltip timings. The before-and-after comparisons are shown visually only; the Figma files linked in the description were not reviewed.
The 'three tells' framing and the claim that AI struggles with hidden UI are the presenter's opinion, not backed by evidence in the video.
Hover-only reveals and hover tooltips assume a pointer; the video does not discuss touch or keyboard access to hidden actions [inferred].
Auto-caption error: 'larger drawers, models' almost certainly means modals [inferred].
